report.headline: Projected NBA usage falls to 14.4%, well below the 20.1% league average, while the shooting-efficiency projection carries no signal.

projection.text: The model projects a 14.4% usage rate in the NBA, down from an 18.2% usage rate in the 2016-17 EuroLeague season, with an 80% prediction interval of 9.1%-19.6% and a 95% interval of 6.4%-22.4%.

risks.text: The 80% prediction interval for usage rate (9.1%-19.6%) spans roughly two standard deviations of the target league's usage distribution (5.2%), meaning the model can rank this player relative to peers but cannot price an individual outcome.
Shot selection featured almost no three-point attempts (0.4% of shots), a profile associated with the typical drop in role seen in the projected fall from 18.2% to 14.4% usage.

No reliable efficiency claim can be made: the true shooting model's error (4.7%) does not improve on assuming league-average shooting (55.7%), so the 55.0% projection should be treated as uninformative.
The projection rests on a thin source sample: the subject was 29.0 years old and played only 993 minutes over 31 games in the source season.

strengths.text: In the source season the subject produced 8.738 rebounds per 75 possessions and 2.466 assists per 75, with a 13.0% assist rate, at a modest 18.2% usage rate, indicating a well-rounded low-usage role.
Source-season true shooting of 60.9% placed the subject +0.60 standard deviations above the EuroLeague average, a strong efficiency mark in context.

The usage rate projection beats the best trivial baseline (3.3% mean absolute error versus 4.3% for the league-mean baseline), so the 14.4% figure carries genuine signal rather than just reflecting league averages.

uncertainty.text: The true shooting projection of 55.0% should not be trusted as informative: the model's 4.7% mean absolute error is no better than the trivial league-mean baseline's 4.7% error, so this figure is effectively just the NBA average (55.7%) restated.
